strengths: The paper introduces an interesting and timely problem setting: personalized 3D head avatars over long life spans rather than momentary captures. This is a meaningful extension of current neural avatar work and is well aligned with computer vision/graphics interests in reconstruction, controllability, and identity consistency from in-the-wild data.

The proposed framework combines a shared canonical 2D Gaussian surfel representation, neural head bases with adaptive pruning (Dynamo), residual lifestage embeddings, and FLAME-driven warping for expression/shape control. While many ingredients are adapted from existing avatar and Gaussian-splatting methods, their integration for lifelong personalized avatar modeling is technically plausible and reasonably motivated.

The manuscript is ambitious in scope and includes a large claimed dataset, TimeWalker-1.0, with 40 celebrity identities and 2.7M frames. The data collection and statistics suggest useful diversity in age, pose, lighting, expression, accessories, and ethnicity, which could provide a valuable benchmark if released responsibly.

Quantitative comparisons on TimeWalker-1.0 and the INSTA-derived setting show clear improvements over several adapted baselines in PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS, especially under the one-model-per-identity lifelong protocol. The ablations on Dynamo/hashgrid count, residual embeddings, and loss terms support the claim that the personalized neural basis design contributes to performance.

The paper includes many qualitative demonstrations: cross-lifestage reenactment, cross-identity driving, mesh reconstruction, lifestage traversal, large-view rendering, lighting interpolation, and downstream 3D editing. These help communicate the capabilities and limitations of the representation.

The authors discuss limitations and broader impact, including failure on tongue/unseen mouth interiors, exaggerated expressions, large yaw angles, preprocessing noise, incomplete lifelong coverage, and misuse risks for deceptive avatar generation.
weaknesses: The evidence for true lifelong generalization is still limited. The main quantitative evaluation uses only 5 identities from the new dataset, despite the dataset containing 40 celebrities, and the train/test split appears to hold out frames from the same lifestages rather than testing more difficult settings such as unseen ages, unseen videos, unseen lighting regimes, or temporally interpolated/extrapolated life stages.

The evaluation relies heavily on image reconstruction metrics from held-out frames. These metrics can reward memorization of correlated video/photo collections and do not directly validate the core claims of disentangled lifelong identity, geometry accuracy, expression transfer fidelity, or age/lifestage controllability. Geometry is mostly evaluated qualitatively; no scan-based, multi-view, landmark, depth, normal, or mesh accuracy metric is reported.

Some baseline comparisons are not fully convincing. PAV is represented by an INSTA++ reimplementation rather than the original method, GPHM is compared only indirectly via metric alignment, and the INSTA dataset experiment treats different individuals as different appearances of the same person, which is an artificial and arguably mismatched proxy for lifelong modeling. These choices make it hard to assess the real margin over the closest prior work.

The dataset raises substantial reproducibility and ethics concerns. It is built from YouTube and movie sources of celebrities, and release is restricted through a non-commercial agreement. Consent, copyright/licensing status, demographic balance beyond coarse categories, identity verification errors, and takedown procedures are not described in sufficient detail. Since the task directly enables realistic identity-specific avatar generation, these issues are central rather than peripheral.

The technical novelty is somewhat incremental at the component level. The method draws heavily on 2D Gaussian surfels, FLAME/INSTA-style inverse warping, hashgrid features, residual embeddings, and 3DMM-style linear bases. The main novelty is their combination for lifelong avatars, but the paper sometimes overstates the conceptual advance relative to existing personalized avatar and appearance-conditioned methods.

The disentanglement claims are not rigorously validated. Lifestage, lighting, expression, shape, and appearance are shown mostly through qualitative interpolation or manipulation, and the paper itself notes that lighting/lifestage separation is imperfect. More controlled evaluations or identity/attribute preservation metrics across manipulations would be needed to substantiate the full-scale controllable-space claim.

The method remains dependent on FLAME fitting, face parsing, pretrained normal/depth priors, matting/cropping quality, and reasonably observed head regions. Failure cases on large pose, mouth interiors, and exaggerated expressions suggest that the approach may be brittle for highly unconstrained lifelong collections, despite the paper's broad framing.

Clarity is generally adequate but the manuscript is very dense and sometimes imprecise. Several terms such as lifestage, moment, appearance, shape, and identity are used interchangeably, and some mathematical details of Dynamo pruning, basis selection, and control at test time are underspecified. The paper would benefit from a cleaner protocol description and stronger separation between claimed capabilities and demonstrated evidence.

strengths: The paper identifies an interesting and underexplored problem: building controllable 3D head avatars from long-term, unstructured photo/video collections rather than from a single capture session.

The proposed system is reasonably complete as an applied avatar pipeline, combining 2D Gaussian surfels, FLAME-based motion control, learnable per-lifestage deformation bases, meshing, reenactment, and editing demonstrations.

The TimeWalker-1.0 collection, if released responsibly, could be useful as a challenging benchmark for cross-age avatar modeling. The paper also includes a broader-impact and ethics discussion and acknowledges some limitations such as FLAME dependence and failure on unseen mouth/tongue regions.

Quantitative results on the authors' dataset show clear improvements over several adapted baselines in PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS, and the ablations support that multiple adaptive hashgrid bases are helpful for the reported reconstruction task.
weaknesses: The central scientific claim, lifelong identity-consistent 3D avatar modeling, is not convincingly evaluated. The main protocol holds out the last 10% of frames from each appearance, which likely tests interpolation within the same videos/conditions rather than true cross-age generalization, unseen lifestages, unseen capture domains, or sparse historical photo settings.

The method is mostly an engineering combination of existing ingredients: Gaussian surfels, FLAME fitting/warping, hashgrid features, residual embeddings, and pruning of low-weight bases. The novelty of Dynamo appears limited, and the paper does not provide a strong technical argument that the learned bases correspond to meaningful identity/lifestage factors rather than memorizing appearance clusters.

The experimental evidence is narrow relative to the claims. Most main results are on only 5 selected identities from a 40-celebrity dataset, with image reconstruction metrics that do not establish 3D geometry quality, identity preservation, temporal consistency, or controllable disentanglement. Mesh comparisons are largely qualitative and lack quantitative geometry evaluation against ground truth.

Baseline comparisons are not fully convincing. Several baselines are adapted in ad hoc ways, PAV is reimplemented as INSTA++, GPHM is not directly compared under the same setting, and one-shot/generative methods are evaluated under protocols that may not reflect their intended use. The paper often concludes superiority over entire method families from limited or non-identical comparisons.

The dataset raises reproducibility and ethics concerns. It is scraped from YouTube/movie sources and celebrities, with unclear consent, copyright status, and train/test release feasibility. The promise of an open benchmark is weakened by the statement that access will be restricted through a usage agreement, and the paper does not specify enough about annotation, age labels, identity filtering errors, or splits to support independent replication.

The paper overclaims. It repeatedly frames the result as full-scale lifelong modeling and comprehensive identity construction, but the data spans mostly age 20-80 celebrities, not actual lifelong coverage, and the limitations admit only preliminary exploration. Failure cases for exaggerated expressions and unseen regions are significant for an avatar animation paper.

Presentation quality is uneven: there are many grammatical issues, inconsistent notation, unclear references to appendix section numbers, and dense figures/tables that make the method and protocols harder to verify. These clarity issues compound the concerns about technical soundness and reproducibility.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and underexplored problem: personalized 3D head avatars across life stages from unstructured photo/video collections. This is a meaningful extension beyond momentary head-avatar reconstruction and is well motivated for computer vision and graphics.

The proposed TimeWalker framework is technically coherent, combining a shared canonical 2D Gaussian Surfel representation with neural head bases, adaptive basis blending, residual embeddings, and FLAME-driven dynamic warping. The formulation gives a plausible path to disentangling lifestage, expression, shape, view, and appearance.

The work includes a substantial new dataset, TimeWalker-1.0, with 40 celebrity identities and 2.7M frames, plus useful statistics on age, pose, brightness, ethnicity, and attributes. This dataset and task framing could serve as a valuable benchmark if released responsibly.

The experimental section is broad: the authors compare against NeRF-based, Gaussian-based, generative, and one-shot avatar baselines; evaluate both single-model and per-lifestage baseline protocols; include ablations for Dynamo, hashgrids, residual embeddings, losses, and multi-lifestage training; and show qualitative results for reenactment, mesh extraction, editing, lighting, and novel views.

The results are convincing enough to show that a single learned personalized space can outperform or match multiple per-stage models on rendering metrics, with particularly strong LPIPS and SSIM. The ablations support the claimed value of adaptive neural bases and multi-lifestage supervision.

The paper is unusually candid about limitations, including failures under extreme expressions, unseen oral regions such as tongue, poor matting/FLAME fits in in-the-wild data, limited age coverage, large-view artifacts, and imperfect lighting disentanglement. The ethics statement acknowledges misuse risks around identity-sensitive avatar assets.
weaknesses: The novelty is partly architectural integration rather than a clean new principle: many components are inherited or adapted from FLAME fitting, INSTA-style inverse warping, hashgrid features, Gaussian Surfels/2DGS, residual embeddings, and standard differentiable rendering losses. The paper would benefit from a sharper explanation of which parts are essential technical advances versus engineering composition.

The term “lifelong” is somewhat overstated. The dataset appears to cover mostly public adult celebrity footage, with ages roughly 20-80 and no true childhood-to-old-age longitudinal capture. The authors acknowledge this, but several claims about lifelong identity modeling should be toned down or evaluated with stronger cross-age protocols.

The main quantitative evaluation uses held-out frames from the same lifestages/videos rather than a rigorous unseen-lifestage or future-age generalization setup. This makes it hard to distinguish genuine cross-age interpolation/generalization from high-quality reconstruction of observed appearance clusters.

Only 5 representative identities are used in the main experiments, and some ablations use 3 or fewer identities. Given that the dataset contains 40 identities, broader quantitative reporting would make the evidence more robust and reduce concern about cherry-picking identities with favorable data distributions.

Several comparisons are imperfect. PAV is not directly compared and is approximated through an INSTA++ reimplementation; GPHM is only compared through aligned metrics rather than a controlled run; one-shot and generative baselines are not always matched to the exact task setting. These choices are understandable but weaken claims of clear SOTA superiority.

The evaluation is dominated by image reconstruction metrics such as PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. For the paper’s central claims, stronger quantitative measures of identity consistency across age, expression controllability, 3D geometry accuracy, temporal/lifestage interpolation quality, and animation fidelity would be valuable.

The method depends heavily on preprocessing quality, including face recognition/cropping, matting, FLAME tracking, face parsing, and monocular normal priors. These dependencies are central failure modes for in-the-wild data but are not fully quantified.

Dataset release and reproducibility remain potential concerns. The paper says it will use a non-commercial license and safeguards, but celebrity-derived identity data raises copyright, consent, privacy, and deepfake risks. The exact release conditions, filtering criteria, and whether all training data can legally be redistributed are not fully clear.
